title: Whose is it?
grammar: Possessives: mijn, jouw, zijn, haar, ons, hun
summary: mijn, jouw/je, uw, zijn, haar, ons/onze, jullie/je, hun. The form depends on the owner only. ons with a het-word in the singular, onze with all others. Also: de fiets van Anna, Anna's fiets. Whose? Van wie is …?
explain:
Possessives (*bezittelijke voornaamwoorden*) say whose something is: my key, her cat, our house. In Dutch the form depends on **the owner** and hardly ever on the thing: `mijn` fiets, `mijn` huis and `mijn` sleutels all use the same word.

### The forms

| owner | possessive | example |
| ik | mijn | mijn sleutel |
| jij / je | jouw / je | jouw kamer |
| u | uw | uw fiets |
| hij, het | zijn | zijn hond |
| zij / ze (she) | haar | haar kat |
| wij / we | ons / onze | ons huis, onze kat |
| jullie | jullie / je | jullie tuin |
| zij / ze (they) | hun | hun spullen |

> Mijn huisgenoot leent vaak mijn spullen. — My housemate often borrows my things.
> Is dit uw portemonnee, meneer? — Is this your wallet, sir?

`je` is the short, unstressed form of `jouw`. Use `jouw` for stress or contrast: `Dat is jouw probleem, niet mijn probleem.` In chats and speech you will also see `m'n` and `z'n` for `mijn` and `zijn`; write the full forms.

### Ons or onze

This is the only possessive that changes with the thing. `ons` goes with a **het-word in the singular**; `onze` goes with every de-word and with every plural.

> Ons huis is oud, maar onze buren zijn heel aardig. — Our house is old, but our neighbours are very nice.

So: `ons konijn`, but `onze konijnen`; `onze kat`, `onze katten`.

### Zijn or haar: look at the owner

`zijn` is for a male owner and for an owner that is a thing or an animal; `haar` is for a female owner. What is owned does not matter. (In formal writing an organisation often gets `haar`: `de gemeente en haar inwoners`.)

> Anna zorgt goed voor haar konijn. — Anna takes good care of her rabbit.
> Peter zoekt zijn oplader. — Peter is looking for his charger.

### Jullie as the subject: usually je

When `jullie` is the subject, the possessive in the same sentence is usually `je`, because jullie … jullie sounds clumsy (it is not wrong). In other sentences `jullie` is the normal possessive.

> Hebben jullie je sleutels bij je? — Do you (plural) have your keys with you?
> Is dit jullie hond? — Is this your (plural) dog?

### Other ways to say whose

- `van` + the owner: `de fiets van Anna`, `de kat van de buren`. This works with every noun and every pronoun, which takes the object form: `van mij`, `van hem`, `van ons`.
- A name + `s`: `Peters auto`. After a, i, o, u or y the s gets an apostrophe, so the vowel keeps its sound: `Anna's fiets`, `Timo's kamer`. This is mainly for names; with other nouns use `van`.

To ask whose something is: `Van wie is …?` The answer uses `van` too.

> Van wie is die oplader? Is hij van jou? — Whose is that charger? Is it yours?
> Dat is van mij. — That is mine.

There are also forms like `de mijne` and `het jouwe` (mine, yours). You will meet them later; for now say `van mij`, `van jou`.

### Hun: their or them

`hun` before a noun means "their": `hun kat`. Unit A2 · 8 also used `hun` (and `hen`) for "them". Recognise the difference: `Dat is hun auto` (their car) against `Ik help hen` (I help them).

### Watch out

- `jouw` is "your", `jou` is "you": `Is dit jouw sleutel?`, never *Is dit jou sleutel?
- The owner decides: `Anna en haar hond`, not *Anna en zijn hond.
- `onze kat`, `onze huizen`, but `ons huis`: never *ons kat or *onze huis.
- No apostrophe after a consonant: `Peters auto`, not *Peter's auto.

### Compared with Ukrainian

`мій, моя, моє, мої` change with the thing; Dutch possessives change only with the owner. And Dutch has **no word for свій**: you always choose the form that fits the owner. `Він любить свою роботу` is `Hij houdt van zijn werk`, `Вона любить свою роботу` is `Zij houdt van haar werk`, `Ми любимо свою роботу` is `Wij houden van ons werk`. Where it could be someone else's, add `eigen` (own): `Hij gebruikt zijn eigen oplader`.

words.en: to take care of / to look after

sentences.nl: Mijn huisgenoot leent vaak mijn spullen.
sentences.en: My housemate often borrows my things.
sentences.note: Mijn is the same for every noun: mijn huisgenoot (de), mijn spullen (plural), mijn huis (het).
alt: Mijn huisgenoot leent mijn spullen vaak.

sentences.nl: Van wie is die oplader? Is hij van jou?
sentences.en: Whose is that charger? Is it yours?
sentences.note: Whose? is Van wie …? and 'yours' is van jou, with the object form after van. De oplader is a de-word, so 'it' is hij.
alt: Van wie is die oplader? Is die van jou?

sentences.nl: Anna zorgt goed voor haar konijn.
sentences.en: Anna takes good care of her rabbit.
sentences.note: The owner is a woman, so haar. That konijn is a het-word does not matter.

sentences.nl: Mijn zus is haar sleutels weer kwijt.
sentences.en: My sister has lost her keys again.
sentences.note: Ukrainian would say свої; Dutch chooses by the owner: mijn zus → haar.

sentences.nl: We delen de keuken, maar we hebben allemaal onze eigen kamer.
sentences.en: We share the kitchen, but we all have our own room.
sentences.note: Kamer is a de-word, so onze. Eigen (own) comes between the possessive and the noun and never changes.

sentences.nl: Ons huis is oud, maar onze buren zijn heel aardig.
sentences.en: Our house is old, but our neighbours are very nice.
sentences.note: Huis is a het-word in the singular: ons. Buren is a plural: onze.

sentences.nl: Hebben jullie je sleutels bij je?
sentences.en: Do you (plural) have your keys with you?
sentences.note: With jullie as the subject, the possessive is usually je; jullie jullie sleutels would sound clumsy.
To someone you call u, the possessive is uw.

sentences.nl: Mijn buren zijn weg, dus ik voer hun kat.
sentences.en: My neighbours are away, so I am feeding their cat.
sentences.note: Hun before a noun means 'their'. Never hen kat: hen only means 'them'.
alt: Mijn buren zijn weg, dus voer ik hun kat.

sentences.en: Today I am borrowing Peter's car.
sentences.note: A name + s shows the owner. Peter ends in a consonant, so there is no apostrophe: Peters.
alt: Ik leen vandaag de auto van Peter.
Vandaag leen ik de auto van Peter.

exercises.nl: Mijn zus zorgt goed voor ___ eigen konijn.
exercises.en: My sister takes good care of her own rabbit.
exercises.note: The owner, mijn zus, is a woman: haar. Konijn is a het-word, but the thing owned does not choose the possessive.

exercises.nl: Wij wonen hier al tien jaar. Dit is ___ huis.
exercises.en: We have lived here for ten years. This is our house.
exercises.note: Huis is a het-word in the singular, so ons. Onze is for de-words and plurals.

exercises.nl: Van wie is de oplader? Is hij van ___?
exercises.en: Whose is the charger? Is it yours?
exercises.note: After van comes the object form jou. Jouw is the possessive and needs a noun after it: jouw oplader.

exercises.nl: De eigenaar van de hond is een oude vrouw. Ze wandelt elke dag met ___ hond.
exercises.en: The owner of the dog is an old woman. She walks with her dog every day.
exercises.note: The owner is a woman, so haar, even though de eigenaar is a de-word. Zijn would mean someone else's dog.
Kat is a de-word, so onze. Ons is only for a het-word in the singular: ons konijn.

exercises.en: The neighbours often borrow our ladder.
exercises.note: Ladder is a de-word, so the possessive of wij is onze.

exercises.nl: Zetten jullie ___ (jullie) fietsen in de gang?
exercises.en: Are you (plural) putting your bikes in the hall?
exercises.note: With jullie as the subject the possessive is usually je. Jullie fietsen is also correct, but sounds heavier.

exercises.nl: Mijn buren zijn op vakantie, dus ik zorg voor ___ (zij, they) konijn.
exercises.en: My neighbours are on holiday, so I am looking after their rabbit.
exercises.note: 'Their' is hun. Hen and ze mean 'them' and cannot stand before a noun.

answers: Dit is de fiets van mijn zus.
exercises.note: With van the owner comes after the thing: de fiets van mijn zus. Only a name can take s: Anna's fiets.

answers: Mijn huisgenoot deelt zijn eten nooit met mij.
Mijn huisgenoot deelt nooit zijn eten met mij.
exercises.en: My housemate never shares his food with me.
exercises.note: The owner of the food is the housemate, a man: zijn eten. After met comes the object form mij.

exercises.task: Use the name with s instead of van.
exercises.from: Dit is de auto van Peter.
exercises.note: Name + s, without an apostrophe after a consonant: Peters auto. The article de disappears.

exercises.task: Use van instead of the name with s.
exercises.from: Mijn oplader is kapot, dus ik leen Anna's oplader.
answers: Mijn oplader is kapot, dus ik leen de oplader van Anna.
exercises.en: My charger is broken, so I am borrowing Anna's charger.
exercises.note: With van the article comes back: de oplader van Anna. Anna's has an apostrophe because the name ends in a.

exercises.task: Change the subject to mijn zus.
exercises.from: Mijn broer zorgt voor zijn konijn.
answers: Mijn zus zorgt voor haar konijn.
exercises.en: My sister looks after her rabbit.
exercises.note: With a new owner the possessive changes too: zijn becomes haar. Dutch has no word like свій that stays the same.

exercises.from: Ik geef mijn huisdieren elke ochtend eten.
answers: Wij geven onze huisdieren elke ochtend eten.
exercises.en: We give our pets food every morning.
exercises.note: Wij needs the plural verb geven, and the possessive follows the owner: onze, because huisdieren is a plural.
'Your' is jouw (or short je). Jou means 'you', as in van jou.

exercises.wrong: Mijn zus heeft nu zijn eigen kamer.
answers: Mijn zus heeft nu haar eigen kamer.
exercises.en: My sister has her own room now.
exercises.note: Eigen means the owner is the subject, mijn zus, so it must be haar. Zijn eigen would only fit a man or a het-word.
